7.2 Financial goals – save now, spend later 
When you plan to save for something over a certain time, you are setting a financial 
goal. Achieving that goal can feel great because you get to buy that special thing you 
wanted. You have also shown that you can be smart with money – a very important life 
skill! Financial goals can be short term, medium term or long term and involve small or 
large amounts of money. 
Answer the following questions about financial goals. You may need a calculator or 
working paper. 
1 
Angelo’s goal: Save $80 over 4 weeks to buy a computer game for his  
brother’s birthday.  
On 1 September 2014, Angelo sets a short-term goal to save $20 every week for  
4 weeks so he can buy the Midas IV game on 29 September 2014 when it is released. 
a Angelo gets $40 pocket money each week. He spends $5 at the 
canteen every school day for lunch and pays $10 a week for his 
mobile phone. What amount does he have left over each week?
b If Angelo takes his own lunch to school for three days of the  
week, how much will he save each week?
c Add your answers to part a and part b. 
d If Angelo saves this amount (part c) each week, can he save $80 
over 4 weeks? 
2 
Liam’ s goal: Save $1248 for an overseas trip. 
On 30 June 2014, Liam sets a medium-term financial goal to save  
for an overseas holiday. He needs to pay for the trip on 2 July 2015.
a If Liam saves from 1 July 2014 to 1 July 2015, how many months 
does he have to save for the trip? 
b How much does he need to save each month? 
(Divide $1248 by the number of months he has to save.)
c If he saves $120 each month, will he have more or less  
than he needs? 
3 
Sandi’s goal: To save $5000 for a deposit on a car by the time she is 21. 
Sandi is 17 and has just passed her driving test. Her long-term goal is to have her  
own car in 4 years’ time. She has just started her final year of school and is working 
part-time. She plans to save $500 over the next 10 months and another $4,500 in the  
3 years after that when she will be working full-time. 
a To save $500 in 10 months, how much must Sandi save each month? 
b To save $4,500 over 3 years, how much must she save each month?
c If Sandi sticks to her plan, how many months will it take to  
achieve her goal?

7.3 Steps to tracking expenses
Read the information below about tracking expenses and answer the following 
question.
Have you ever checked your wallet or your bank balance and found you had way less 
money than you thought you did? Did you wonder where it all went because you can’t 
remember spending that much? Even worse, have you found that you didn’t have enough 
money to go out, pay a bill or couldn’t afford to buy something you really wanted? 
To achieve financial goals, you need to make a written plan that shows how much money 
is coming in and how you plan to spend this money. This is called budgeting. When your 
income is more than your expenses, you can save money. 
The first step to budgeting is tracking expenses. This allows you to 
see what you usually spend your money on. To track your expenses, 
keep a record of everything you pay for or buy for a month or two. 
Then sort your spending into different categories or groups, 
such as food, transport, entertainment and clothing. 
You can track expenses by using an application on your 
mobile phone, writing in a notebook, keeping receipts or 
using a spreadsheet on your computer. Tracking expenses 
is easier if you use only one or two methods of payment, 
such as cash and debit card only, and avoid credit cards. 
Once you can see where all your money is going, you can make 
budgeting decisions about how much to spend on each category 
and how much you can save. Governments, businesses, families 
and individuals all track expenses so they can take control of 
their money, build budgets and achieve financial goals.

a  A budget is a written plan that shows money coming in and how

b  You should track your expenses for a day or two before developing 
a budget.
c  To save money, your expenses should be more than your income.
d  Notebooks, mobile phones and spreadsheets can all be used to 
track expenses.
e  When you track your expenses, you can see exactly how much you 
spend in a week or a month on a category such as ‘entertainment’. 
f  It is better to use more than two different methods of payment to 
help you track your spending.

A budget is simply a written plan for how you intend to spend your money over a 
certain time. Preparing a budget allows you to balance your income and expenses by 
setting a limit on your spending in different categories. A good budget also allows for 
savings. This money is put aside for special purchases and emergency situations, such 
as being sick and unable to work or having large unexpected bills.
Look at Karl’s budget plan below. He is in Year 10, receives an allowance and has 
a casual job washing cars. Note Karl’s expenses and the limits he has set for his 
spending in each category. He also has a savings category.

A great way to find out how budgeting works is by learning about the envelope system 
of budgeting. This system is useful for people who use cash and don’t have many costly 
expenses. It is flexible, easy to use and helps with understanding the basics of budgeting.

How does it work? 
Karl gets paid in cash, so each week he puts the 
planned amounts of money into separate labelled 
envelopes. When he needs to spend money at 
the school canteen, he takes it out of the food 
and drink envelope. He is careful to spread his 
spending over the week as he knows that when 
that money in the envelope is spent, he will have 
to wait until his next pay to fill it up again. He also 
uses the envelopes for keeping receipts and records 
his purchases on the front of each envelope. 
At the end of the week, Karl transfers any money 
left over to the following week. For example, if 
he doesn’t spend money on clothes in week 1, he 
has an extra $10 to spend on clothes in week 2. 
He can also transfer unspent money into different 
categories if necessary. So, if he doesn’t spend any 
money on transport, the next week he can use that 
money for extra entertainment. 
Another great thing about this budget system is that 
it allows for savings. Karl puts $35 into his savings 
envelope each week. Then he deposits this money 
into his bank account so it earns interest. This 
will help him to achieve his financial goal to save 
$3000 by the time he leaves school in 2015.

2.2 Where’s the best place to shop?
Read the information about places to shop. Then answer the following questions.
There are many different options and locations to buy 
from when shopping. The best place for a customer to 
shop depends on what they want to buy. Some customers 
want to spend time looking for the perfect option. In 
this case, a shopping centre where lots of different 
stores are grouped together would be the best place to 
shop. Customers who want to find the perfect item can 
look online where stores from Australia and around the 
world all sell their items, often at a cheaper price.
Customers who value convenience could choose to buy all their items from one store. 
Department stores and supermarkets sell many different kinds of items including food, 
clothing, technology, furniture, stationery and much more.
Customers looking for something unique or second-hand can also find the perfect place 
to shop. Opportunity shops, commonly known as ‘op shops’, offer second-hand items at a 
good price. Many markets also offer previously owned or cheap items for sale. However, 
customers at these locations may have to spend more time looking and sorting through 
items to find the perfect product.

Marcus buys a new set of golf clubs. The original price of the golf clubs was $1,500 but 
when Marcus went to the register to pay, the retail assistant reduced the price  
to $1,400. What percentage discount did Marcus receive?
 
original price – amount paid = $ discount
 
$1,500 – $1,400 = $100 discount
 
$ discount ÷ original price = decimal discount
 
$100 ÷ $1,500 = 0.067
 
decimal discount × 100 = % discount
 
0.067 × 100 = 6.7% discount
 rounded up to the next whole number = 7% discount
2.3 How much is the discount?
Read the information about calculating discounts. Then answer the following 
questions. You will need a calculator or working paper.
People often purchase things because they get discounts. A discount is when an amount of 
money is taken off the price you pay. The larger the discount you get, the cheaper the price! 
A discount is often shown as a percentage of the total price, such as 10% or 25%.
It’s hard to judge the best value if you’re not sure how much you save with a discount. The 
examples below show you how to figure it out. 
Tip: If your answer ends in 
a decimal, round it to the 
nearest whole number. 
•  If your answer ends in .5 or 
above, such as 4.6, 5.8 or 
10.9, round up to the next 
whole number. 
•  If your answer ends in .4

3.2 Paying with cash versus credit
Read the information about cash, credit and debit cards. Then answer the question. 
 
1 
Are these statements true or false? If you answer false, edit the statement to make it true.
Statement
True or 
false?
a You must be 16 years old to get a credit card in Australia.
b Cash is not always accepted as a method of payment.
c A major disadvantage of credit is that it is more expensive to 
use than cash.
d Storing funds electronically is often safer than cash.
e Using cash can sometimes attract surcharges.
f Credit cards and debit cards allow people to spend more 
money than they actually have.
Why should I pay cash?
For many years, cash has been the preferred way of paying for the things we want to 
buy. It is something everyone recognises and when we see a note or coin we all know 
the value it holds. Cash has many other benefits over credit or debit cards.
First of all, anyone can use cash, no matter what their age. This is not the case for 
credit cards or debit cards. In Australia, you must be 18 years old to apply for a credit 
card. While there is no age restriction for debit cards, teenagers usually need their 
parent’s approval to get one. The main difference between a debit card and credit card 
is that a debit card uses your own money whereas a credit card is a form of borrowing 
money to pay for items. Neither credit cards nor debit cards are as simple to use  
as cash.
Secondly, cash is simple. If you only pay in cash, there is less chance of spending 
more than you can afford. This can easily happen with credit cards which often have 
a large limit on the amount you can spend, as well as high interest rates.
Cash is also always accepted. Some places may not accept credit or debit cards or 
require you to spend a certain amount of money before you can use them. This often 
means that people spend more just so they can pay using their cards.
Credit and debit cards also attract extra fees. This means that sometimes a product 
is more expensive because a charge or surcharge is added to the cost of the purchase.
Sometimes you get a discount for paying with cash. This is because businesses 
don’t have to pay the credit/debit card surcharge. That makes the product cheaper  
for you.
Cash does have disadvantages. One major problem with cash is that it can be lost 
or stolen. If you use a credit card or debit card, even if the card is lost the funds stored 
electronically are still safe.

3.6 Card fraud
Vanessa recently received a letter about debit and credit card fraud.  
She has some questions about the information.  
Read the letter and answer Vanessa’s questions on the next page.
16 November 2014
Dear Vanessa,
As Christmas approaches, we understand that many of our customers start 
using their debit and credit cards more frequently. This includes shopping 
in-store, but also Internet shopping. You may have recently made purchases 
over the Internet, whether it be buying presents for friends overseas or 
concert tickets for that next big event. But there are some important facts for 
you to know about fraud and how it could affect you.
What is fraud?
Fraud is defined as a form of deception used in order to gain financially or 
personally. In most cases, it involves criminals stealing information like card 
details and using them to pay for items with your money.
There are many different kinds of fraud. The two most common examples in 
Australia are:
•  card not present fraud: card details are used to complete transactions via 
phone, fax, mail or the Internet
•  counterfeit card fraud: a fake card is used to make purchases.
Card fraud is affecting a growing number of people due to increased online 
shopping and purchasing from overseas, where laws are not as strict as in 
Australia. An increase in hacking (using a computer to access and steal 
personal data) around the world may also contribute to increasing fraud 
rates.
How can you tell if you are a victim of fraud?
These signs may indicate the occurrence of fraud:
• unknown transactions appearing on your bank statement
• recently providing your credit card details to someone untrustworthy
•  amounts that differ from the actual amounts spent on purchases appearing 
from retailers on your bank statement. (Note that items purchased 
overseas may appear at different values in the bank statement due to the 
conversion of currency.)

4.2 Who is buying apps?
‘Appy customers spend big
The little programs that we download 
frequently are now big business for 
technology companies around the world.
Applications, commonly known as ‘apps’, are 
small pieces of software downloaded onto 
devices such as mobile phones and tablets 
that enable users to access additional features. 
These features could be in the form of games, 
news sites, weather reports or even programs 
enabling cheap international phone calls.
The year 2012 saw a huge rise in the creation 
and purchase of apps. There are now hundreds 
of thousands of apps available for purchase 
by customers. With so much choice, it makes 
the world of apps a confusing, and sometimes 
expensive place. While most apps are free 
and those that are not cost only a few dollars, 
the purchase of multiple apps in a week can 
still hurt the wallets of customers. The 
downloading of large file sizes of apps can 
cost customers even more – particularly if they 
go over their Internet download limits set by 
Internet providers.
The majority of smart phone users also use apps 
in today’s technology-obsessed world. But with 
the increase in apps, there has also been an 
increase in costs. These days, it is estimated 
the average smart phone user spends less than 
$20 a month on applications. 
So what are customers spending their money 
on? The most common apps downloaded are 
games. Many people believe this is because 
most users of apps are young people who use 
them for entertainment. This doesn’t mean 
that apps are just for kids though. There are 
also apps designed to help customers learn or 
provide them with valuable information.
App-user Jordan Coleman, a 42-year-old 
physiotherapist, says that the apps he uses 
‘help him to do almost everything in life.’ The 
apps he listed as being useful included a 
restaurant guide, language lessons, an alarm 
clock and sleep monitor and a train schedule 
which is ‘more useful and gives more accurate 
information than the employees at the train 
station’. When asked how much he would pay 
for an app, he responded, ‘If I used it every 
day? I would pay at least $20.’
Goes to show that apps aren’t just for the kids.

4.5 Why is piracy illegal?
Not even three weeks into the New 
Year and already one of Australia’s 
largest retailers is feeling the sting 
of online downloads on their sales 
and profits. 
Australian Sales Manager of General 
Mart, Peter Gibson, said figures over 
the Christmas holiday season, were 
‘slow, especially in CD and DVD 
sales’. He blames poor sales figures 
on the rise in customers downloading 
content both legally and illegally.
‘We did see a huge increase in 
the sales of prepaid cards which 
customers 
can 
use 
to 
legally 
download music, films, books and 
other content,’ Peter Gibson said.
It is the illegal download industry 
that is causing retailers to panic. 
Worldwide, illegal downloads of 
music alone costs billions of dollars 
each year, let alone downloads 
of all the other kinds of content. 
When asked in a recent survey, 
most people said the reason they 
download content illegally is because 
they think one download won’t have 
much impact. Another reason often 
given is that music and films are 
too expensive to buy, especially for 
young people, so illegal downloading 
is the only option.
An important fact many pirates 
(people who choose to download 
content illegally) don’t consider is 
the way in which their piracy affects 
others. For example, if one person 
downloads a music album illegally, it 
means that music artists are not paid 
the money their artistic skill entitles 
them to. Many others lose money 
that is rightfully theirs, including 
songwriters, 
lawyers, 
marketers, 
sound engineers, musicians and 
even retailers like General Mart.
Governments around the world are 
trying new measures to prevent 
illegal 
downloads 
from 
ruining 
jobs 
and 
businesses. 
Penalties 
for downloading illegally can now 
include fines and, for some of the 
biggest offenders, jail sentences. 
These penalties are yet to be tested 
in Australia and no pirates have 
been jailed over this crime to date. 
However, in the United States, some 
pirates have been fined hundreds 
of thousands of dollars for illegally 
downloading just one or two albums 
from the Internet. Many people 
argue this harsh punishment does 
not fit the small crime committed.
As sales of CDs and DVDs decrease, 
retailers like General Mart are now 
faced with a tough decision: do they 
continue to stock CDs and DVDs in 
their stores or is it not worth it?
Peter Gibson admits, ‘We will be 
reducing the number of CDs and 
DVDs we offer to customers in our 
stores and hope customers come in 
and continue to purchase prepaid 
cards from us to download items 
legally.’
Another store bites the dust
Graeme Williams

5.1 What are shopping scams?
Read the information about shopping scams below then complete the following 
crossword and questions.
Common shopping scams
Every time we shop, we trust that the people we buy products from are telling us the truth. 
In some cases, the people we buy from may be untrustworthy scammers. They may sell us 
products of a lesser quality than we expect, or try to charge a higher price. 
One common scam is ‘double ticketing’. This is where a product has two price tags on it. 
When a customer takes the item to the register, the store charges the more expensive price 
even though they know it should be sold for the cheaper price.
Another common scam is ‘bait and switch’. This is where stores advertise a product for a 
very attractive price. When the customer comes into the store to buy the product they are 
told it is ‘sold out’ and offered a similar, more expensive product instead. What makes this 
dishonest is the fact that they might never have stocked the original product, or stocked 
only a few items so it sold out faster than customers would expect it to.
As more people start shopping online, the number of scams is increasing. Online 
anonymous sellers can use false or insecure websites to steal credit card information and 
money. Once scammers have your money, they could send you faulty products, products 
different to what you ordered or sometimes no product at all! 
In the case of online auction shopping, scammers can put fake bids on products to drive  
the prices up and make genuine customers pay more. These fake bids might be done by  
the seller themselves or by other people involved in the scam who are known as  
‘dummy bidders’.

One of the top tips to prevent being scammed is to make further enquiries about products 
if you have doubts about it. An enquiry can be in the form of a letter, email, online form

Tips for structuring your enquiry
•  Format your enquiry like a standard letter. 
A professional enquiry is more likely to 
receive a professional reply.
•  Use clear and concise language. Don’t ask 
long questions. If necessary, break complex 
questions into parts or dot points.
•  Introduce your enquiry by listing the item 
you wish to discuss. Some sellers may have 
multiple items they are selling online.
•  Always be specific when asking questions.

colour the product is, ask for specific shades.

The goods we buy at stores do not always last the way we expect them to. Sometimes, 
we purchase goods that don’t work as they should or are faulty. According to Australian 
law, there are two major kinds of faults that can occur in goods: major faults and  
minor faults.
Read the information below about faulty goods then answer the following 
questions.
7.2 When is a good faulty?
Major faults versus minor faults
A major fault is a problem with a good that means you wouldn’t have 
bought it if you had known about the problem. Imagine you purchased 
a new mountain bike and when you rode it for the first time you found 
out that the gears didn’t change! This is an example of a major fault.
A fault can be considered major if any one of the following occurs:
• The goods are different from the description given.
•  The goods are not fit for their usual purpose; that is, the goods 
don’t do what they are meant to do.
• The goods are unfit for a purpose that you told the seller about.
• The goods are unsafe for use.
All other faults with products are classified as minor faults. Examples of 
minor faults include a car that runs well but has some scratches on the 
paint, or clothing with stitching that is not quite straight.
Remedies for faults
Remedy is a legal term used for an action 
that corrects a wrong. In the case of major 
and minor faults, remedies ensure that the 
customer does not lose money or use an 
unsafe product.
The three most common remedies for faults 
are refunds, repairs and exchanges. A 
refund is when the customer returns an 
item to the seller and receives the money 
they originally paid for the item. A repair 
to the product may include new parts or 
components to return it to working order. 
An exchange may be for a newer, working 
version of the original product, or for credit 
that can be used to buy other goods.
In the case of a major fault, the customer 
chooses which remedy they want. For minor 
faults, the business chooses the remedy.

7.5 What remedies are available?
Read the information about remedies and answer the following questions.
The three major remedies available to customers are refunds,  
repairs and exchanges. Each remedy offers its own advantages  
and disadvantages.
In the case of refunds, the customer returns the faulty item and 
receives the money they originally paid for it. Refunds can be 
in cash, credit (refunded onto debit or credit cards) or in the form of store credit which 
allows the customer to return to the store later to purchase another item. A major advantage 
of cash or credit refunds is that the customer receives the remedy more quickly. This can 
benefit both the customer and the store as the customer often feels they have received 
better service and may be more likely to return to the store to make future purchases. 
Offering store credit is even better for the store as it ensures the customer will return and 
spend their money there, rather than at a different store. In the case of a major fault, the 
customer can choose the remedy they want, including the type of refund.
Repairs can be both simple and complex. Some repairs can be done in-store and may be 
as simple as using a special tool to change batteries in a product. Other repairs can take 
longer. In some cases, the good may have to be sent to another store, another state, or even 
another country! People are more likely to choose repair when the item is rare, they want to 
keep that particular item or the item has personal significance.
An exchange is probably the simplest form of remedy. It is most commonly done when the 
customer still wants to own the item and another one is available in the store. The store 
simply swaps the faulty item for a working version.

8.1 Tips for making a complaint
1 
Use the information above to make a list of the right and wrong ways to complain.
The right way to complain
The wrong way to complain
When you find that goods are faulty, it is common sense to return them to the store or 
manufacturer. If you are not satisfied with the quality of an item, you have the right to 
complain. This can be done in many ways. Usually, people visit the store they bought the 
item from. You can also complain by phone, email or letter. Whichever way you choose, 
it is important to know the right way to complain.
When returning a faulty item it is important to remain calm. Becoming aggressive 
when complaining about items only makes it more difficult to communicate with the 
salesperson. Stay composed and be patient with the salesperson you are complaining to.
It also helps to write down information if you are dealing with a large complaint. This 
is especially important when dealing with complaints in-store or over the phone. Keep 
records of who you speak to and when, and what was agreed. This helps avoid any 
confusion later.
If you are not happy with the solution first offered, it is perfectly fine to ask to speak to 
someone else. If you want to, ask to speak to a manager. If the manager is not in the store 
or is otherwise unavailable, ask for them to contact you when they can. 
If the response you receive in-store or over the phone is  
unsatisfactory, it may help to write a letter. This also  
means that all the important information is written  
down in one place for future reference. Make sure  
any letters you send are factual and reasonable.  
Don’t make false accusations or threats. 
In your letter, explain your rights under law.  
Also make sure you offer a way for the store  
or manufacturer to contact you. If you don’t  
provide contact information, you can’t expect  
the complaint to be addressed!
Finally, only as a last resort, seek legal advice regarding the complaint.  
Never threaten to sue or take a store to court straight away!

8.2 Analyse a complaint letter
1 
Read the descriptions of the parts of a complaint letter. 
A: Explain your rights.
When you understand your legal rights 
you have a better chance of getting the 
resolution you want. If a product has 
a major fault, explain your rights to 
refund, repair or exchange.
B: Explain the problem.
Clearly describe the problem with the 
product in as much detail as you can.
C: Include contact information.
Be sure to tell the person how and 
when is best to contact you in order to 
solve the problem you are complaining 
about.
D:  Name, title and address of 
person receiving the complaint
If possible, use the full name and 
job title of the person receiving the 
complaint to make sure it reaches the 
right person at the organisation.
E: Greeting and introduction
Use the name of the person you are 
addressing the complaint to. Introduce 
the product you wish to complain 
about, list when and where it was 
purchased and make reference to any 
proof of purchase you may have to 
support your claim.
F: Offer a solution
Outline the remedy or solution you 
want – it may be a refund, repair or 
exchange of the faulty good.
G: Sign off the letter
Include a formal farewell and your 
full name at the bottom of the letter.
H:   Provide information about 
previous interactions
In most cases, letters are written as 
a second step after visiting the store 
and trying to resolve the complaint 
in person. If a previous attempt to 
solve the problem has occurred, 
explain it to the person now 
handling the complaint.

Who am I?
4a
I am one of Australia’s oldest industries. While once
Australia was ‘riding on its back’, in recent years the industry
has experienced decline. Australia, is still however the
world’s largest producer, accounting for over a quarter of
world production.
4b
I am the second largest settlement in NSW after Sydney.
I am a river port which specialises in bulk cargo, with my
biggest export being coal.
4c
I am an isolated mining town, located 838 kilometres
north of Cairns. I was built for the purpose of mining bauxite,
which is mined, washed, graded and loaded here for
shipment to an aluminium processing plant at Gladstone.
4d
Due to globalisation and trade liberalisation, I have
experienced substantial decline in recent decades as I am no
longer able to compete globally.
4e
I have experienced growth in recent decades and am a
substantial contributor to Australia’s exports and gross
domestic product. I was given a boost by Australia’s hosting
of the Olympics and the Rugby World Cup.
4f
This industry has experienced spectacular growth in
recent years. Australia now ranks in the top six producers in
the world. Our top three producing zones are the Lower
Murray (SA), Big Rivers (NSW) and North West Victoria.

tectonic or gradation forces.

gradation. Erosional features are created where material has
been removed, while depositional features consist of material
relocated following its erosion. In the table below match the
following landforms with their description, and indicate if they

Introduction
Landform refers to the shape of the earth’s surface, and is the result of processes operating both beneath
the earth surface (tectonic forces) and those affecting the land from above (gradational forces). Tectonic forces usually force the
surface upwards or change its structure, while gradation forces usually break it down and even out the level of the land. Individual
landform features are often classified into residual, erosional or depositional by the way these gradational forces have affected the
initial surface.

Elevation
Australia is the lowest and flattest of all the continents. This is
because it is located almost centrally on a crustal plate, with
no major mountain-building activity that commonly occurs
where plates join. The ancient rocks have therefore been
subjected to gradational forces for much longer than on other
continents.

Introduction
Australia’s low rainfall and the distribution of water resources are the most important factors determining our
settlement pattern, landuse and rural production. A scarcity of both surface and groundwater resources places significant
limitations on our use of this continent that can only partially be overcome with modifications such as dams and reservoirs.
Although our main river system, the Murray–Darling, ranks as the world’s 15th longest, its discharge (the volume of water flowing
through it) is among the lowest for the world’s major river systems. Recent and current water shortages and restrictions on water
use in Australian towns and cities have highlighted our water resource problems.

Introduction
Air masses are large bodies of air with relatively uniform horizontal qualities of temperature and moisture,
which they acquire from that part of the earth’s surface over which they form (their source region). Air masses are moved about by
winds, and interact with pressure systems and the topography of the land to bring changes in weather when a different air mass
arrives. Dominating air masses also create typical seasonal weather in some parts of Australia.

Introduction
Weather refers to the short-term, day-to-day changes in the condition of the atmosphere, while climate
involves the longer-term or annual patterns of weather. Many aspects of our daily lives and the operation of our society and
industries are influenced by the weather. Pressure systems are a basic determinant of weather. In lows, the air rises and cools
tending to create cloud, while in highs it descends and warms, bringing fine weather. Between the cells of pressure, surface winds
move air masses from one place to another, creating changes in the weather. The pressure systems (and air masses) tend to
migrate north and south with the seasons, creating distinct seasonal changes in the weather, known as climate.

Australia’s pattern of vegetation is the result of it’s geologic history, past and present climate, location and
size, and the impacts of its inhabitants. Land clearing and vegetation modification have accelerated to the extent that we now
need replanting, pest eradication and forest protection programs. These programs are an acknowledgment of the value of our flora
to our environment, economy and society.

Introduction
Australia is particularly prone to the hazards of drought and bushfire. Our location under a zone of eastward
migrating highs or anticyclones and the El Nino phenomenon combine to limit our rainfall and make drought a frequent problem.

terms of their specific causes, spatial extent, duration, the degree to which we can predict and prepare for them, and the effects
they have on our people, economy and environment.

NATI
VE T
ITLE
Introduction
Native Title is the recognition under Australian law that indigenous people prior to European settlement had
a system of law and ownership of their land. This recognition finally came about in 1992 as a result of the High Court’s Mabo
decision. Until this time the doctrine of terra nullius had prevailed.
a
When all people with an interest in the area covered by a Native Title claimant
application are brought together by the Native Title Tribunal to discuss their own interests
in that area and the interests of others.
b
The decision of the High Court of Australia in 1992 which recognised that the Meriam
people had Native Title over their lands.
c
The existence and exercise of Native Title rights alongside the rights of others to areas
of land or waters.
d
Land belonging to the government.
e
The rights and interests of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in land and
waters according to their traditional laws and customs that are recognised under
Australian law.
f
Outright land ownership.
g
An independent body established under the Native Title Act 1993 to assist people to
resolve Native Title issues.
h
Land leased from a state government or the Northern Territory government for the
purposes of pastoral activity.
i
The idea that the Australian continent belonged to no one at the time of European
arrival.
j
The decision of the High Court of Australia in 1996, which states that the grant of a
pastoral lease does not necessarily extinguish Native Title and that Native Title rights
may coexist with the rights of some leaseholders.

Introduction
Although Australia began its European history as an urban society, it developed into an important
agricultural producer as settlement spread both inland and along the coasts. More recently, mining and manufacturing increased in
relative importance, with the latest era being dominated by services. The distribution of agriculture has always been heavily
dependent on biophysical factors. Manufacturing location varies, with some activities influenced strongly by mineral, rural produce
or energy supplies and others being market oriented. Services dominate in our large urban centres.

Introduction
Trade is an essential regional and global link for Australia. It allows us to export products in which we have
a competitive advantage and import products which we are less efficient at producing. The Australian government pursues a
multilateral (through its membership of the World Trade Organisation), regional (through its membership of regional organisations
such as APEC) and bilateral (through negotiation of specific free trade agreements) approach to trade policy.

trade among its members by 2010 for developed countries and 2020 for developing
countries.

between themselves.

computer equipment and telecommunications equipment.

the country to which they are exported

Australia because of its focus on reductions for agricultural protection.

A global organisation, dealing with the rules of trade between nations. It was
established in 1995 to replace GATT. It has 148 member nations, accounting for 97%

Introduction
As the world economy continues to grow, newly emerging prosperity in some of the most populous
nations, such as China, will add substantially to the demand for energy. Pressure on the existing energy sources will increase, as
will the need to expand alternative supplies.
Definitions
renewable – those resources which
due to continuous natural supply, recycling or reproduction
continue to be available despite human use. For some
resources, this depends on the rate of human use being
slower than the rate of natural replacement.
non-renewable – those resources which are in fixed,
limited or finite in supply and once used are not replaced
by natural processes (except after very long periods of
geologic time). Some of these may be capable of recycling
after human use to extend the period of their use.

Introduction
Freshwater is a universal necessity. It sustains all forms of life, allowing ecosystems to operate by providing
food, recycling energy and removing waste. For humans, water also promotes development. Without adequate supplies, living
standards decline, people suffer and economic growth declines. To focus the world’s attention on current and growing water-
related issues, the UN declared 2003 the International Year of Freshwater.
Definition
Term

river or aquifer
2 Freshwater that is regularly replenished by the hydrologic cycle for withdrawal within reasonable
time limits.
3 A layer or section of earth or rock that contains freshwater (groundwater)
4 A situation where a country has an annual per capita water supply of 1000 to 1700 cubic metres
and will experience temporary or limited water shortage
5 Water in aquifers or other natural sources that is not recharged or recharges so slowly by natural
processes that its withdrawal by humans causes depletion
6 A situation where a country has an annual per capita waster supply of less than 1000 cubic metres
and will experience chronic and widespread supply problems that hinder development
7 A term for water/systems that reduce health risk to humans, such as sewage disposal and drainage
aquifer, non-renewable water, renewable water, sanitation, water withdrawal, water scarcity, water stress

The amount (and quality) of water available for human use
varies markedly due to natural availability from the water
cycle, population levels and availability of technology to
protect, treat and transport the available water.

Introduction
Tropical rainforests are found in the warm wet climates of the tropics. They are vitally important, not only
for their biodiversity – over half the world’s plant and animal species live in rainforests – but for the role they play in regulating

deforestation.

Introduction
The traditional ‘demographic transition’ model of population considered only birth and deathrates. Initially,
populations were kept small by high birth and high deathrates, then falling deathrates led to rapid population growth. Birthrates
then began to fall until a final stage of low growth or stability was reached. Countries were seen to pass through these stages with
increasing economic development. This unit explores some of the factors influencing population change and uses recent United
Nations data to compare what is happening in the more and less developed regions of the world.

China’s One Child Policy was introduced in 1979. Up until this time, the Chinese government had been
encouraging its population to have children. However, by the 1970s a realisation had come about that if the country was going to
develop and improve the economic circumstances of its people it would need to limit population growth.

In order to interpret a population pyramid there are a number of features of population pyramids that you should be aware of:

∑Age categories are generally broken down into 5-year groupings, such as 0–4, and so on.

How does the One Child Policy work?
∑Each workplace has a quota of the number of women who can get pregnant in a given year. Before having a child a woman must
inform her work unit that she is planning on having a baby and will only be given permission if the yearly quota is not yet full.
∑Incentives are used to encourage women to sign the One Child pledge such as an extra month’s salary per year until the child is
14 or larger houses.
∑Penalties are used if a woman breaks the One Child pledge such as a demotion at work or job loss, enforced abortions and
sterilisations.
∑If people have a second child without permission, it cannot be registered and therefore cannot legally attend school and will have
difficulty in obtaining permission to marry in the future.
∑While in cities most couples are restricted to one child, in some rural areas if the first child is a girl couples can seek permission
to try a second time to have a son. The government accepts that in rural areas a son is needed to inherit the land and look after
elderly parents.
Effects of the One Child Policy
∑A significant drop in fertility. In the 1970s, China’s fertility rate was 5.8 babies per woman, but is now at 1.7 babies per woman.
Fertility has dropped to below the level to replace the population.
∑A huge gender imbalance. Due to a cultural preference for sons, parents have used ultrasound tests to detect and selectively
abort daughters. The latest census found 117 male newborns for every 100 females.
∑Female infanticide. There have been many reports of baby girls being starved, abandoned or dumped.
∑A generation of little emperors. Many people believe the One Child Policy has created a generation of pampered, over-indulged
only children.
∑The ageing of China’s population.
∑Human rights abuses. Many people feel that China’s One Child Policy is an abuse of human reproductive rights.

Despite international efforts to reduce
poverty, hunger is on the rise again
after falling steadily during the first
half of the 1990s, according to the
annual FAO report, ‘State of Food
Insecurity in the World’.
Almost 850 million people go to
bed hungry every night, the vast
majority in Africa and Asia, while the
number of hungry people in the
developing world is climbing at a rate
of almost 5 million a year, according
to the UN.
At the UN World Food Summit in
1996, governments set a goal of
cutting in half the number of hungry
people by 2015, using 1990–2 as a
base-line. The FAO said it was time
nations examined why hundreds of
millions of people went hungry in a
world that produced more than
enough food for everyone. ‘Bluntly
stated, the problem is not so much a
lack of food as a lack of political will,’
the report says.
Except when wars or natural
disasters put a spotlight on
developing countries, ‘little is said and
less is done’ to end the plight of the
798 million people who suffer from
chronic hunger, the report says.
Another 11 million people in the
developed countries and 34 million in
countries in transition are hungry.
According to the FAO report,
during the first half of the 1990s, the
number of chronically hungry people
decreased by 37 million. But since
1995–7, the number has increased by
18 million. A closer analysis of the
figures revealed ‘an even more
alarming trend’ – that the number of
hungry people in the developing world
increased by 4.5 million a year
between 1995 and 2001.
About 19 countries reduced the
number of hungry people since
1990–2 by a total of over 80 million.
Twenty-two countries, including
Bangladesh, Haiti and Mozambique
‘turned the tide’ against hunger, in the
second half of the decade.
At the other end of the scale are
26 countries where hunger increased
by almost 60 million, including
Afghanistan, Congo, Burundi, North
Korea, Somalia, Tanzania,
Guatemala, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

1 A person, who leaves a country voluntarily to seek a better life in a new country would be considered
a refugee.
2 In January 2002, 18% of the world’s refugees were from Africa.
3 An internally displaced person is someone who has lost their home but remains inside their country.
4 A person who has fled their country of origin because they were tortured for speaking out against their
government would be considered a refugee.
5 A group of people, who have fled political persecution, but remain within their country are known as
asylum seekers.

7 The number of refugees worldwide has continuously increased since 1980.
Protecting refugees – the Geneva Convention
The 1951 Geneva Convention relating to the status of refugees is the key legal document in defining a refugee. It outlines the rights
and responsibilities of both the refugees and the states that are parties to the convention. It was originally focussed on Europe, then
strengthened and expanded worldwide by the 1967 protocol. By 2004 there were 142 states that were parties to the convention.

GNI – gross national income. The sum of the value added by all resident producers in an economy, plus receipts of primary
income from foreign sources.
OECD – Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development
Introduction
International Aid comes from a variety of government and non-government sources and exists in a range of
forms from financial assistance at the national level to food and clothing in a disaster at the local level. However, it is a
controversial aspect of human development. Criticisms include concerns over the amount of aid being given by nations,
approaches to providing aid, lack of accountability, the donor benefiting more than the recipient and the imposition of a Western
model of development on developing nations.
bilateral aid, emergency aid, multilateral aid, non-government organisation, official development assistance, project aid, tied aid,
untied aid

4

technical assistance being provided.
5
A voluntary not for profit organisation that accepts donations from the public and provides aid to
developing countries through specific projects.
6
Grants, loans, goods and services given by the government of developed nations to assist the
development of developing countries.
7
Where a country receiving aid in the form of money is free to spend it in a way that they choose.
8
When the donor country sets conditions on how the recipient country must spend the aid.

Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
We use electrical energy to power our homes, 
schools and places of work. Generating 
electricity by burning coal or gas in a power 
station is not sustainable, and produces carbon 
dioxide. Using sunlight to make electricity 
is sustainable. A solar panel is a grid of 
photovoltaic cells that convert sunlight  
into electric power. 
Power is measured in watts.  
One kilowatt (kW) = 1000 watts (W). 
A single solar panel produces between  
100 and 200 watts, depending on the brand  
and size. A system of several panels can be 
installed on a house roof to generate some  
or all of the energy used by the household.
1

a 1 kW 
b 3 kW
2

What is the total power generated? Answer in kilowatts. 
3

There are 1000 millimetres (mm) in one metre (m).
a What is the area of the panel in square millimetres? 
b Converting to metres, the panel measures               m long by               m wide. 
c What is the panel’s area in square metres?
d How many square millimetres are there in one square metre? 
4 
A solar energy system installed on a school roof is made up of ten 200 W panels,  
each 1.8 m long and 1.1 m wide. The roof is a rectangle 30 m long and 8 m wide.
a What is the area of one solar panel in square metres? 
b What area of the roof is covered by solar panels?
c What is the area of the roof?
d What percentage of the roof area is covered with solar panels?
e How many whole panels will fit across 30 metres of roof if each panel is 1.1 m wide  
and they are laid side-by-side?
f A maximum of four rows of panels can be fitted onto the roof.  
How many panels will that be?

Wind is an important source of sustainable 
energy. A wind turbine uses the wind to turn 
its large blades, which drive an electricity 
generator at the top of the tower. Electric 
cables carry the electricity to the  
mains grid. 
Wind farms range from a community 
wind farm with a few turbines, to large 
commercial farms of several hundred 
turbines. 
Wind farms are sited in areas of high wind, 
such as upland ridges and the west coasts 
of Victoria and Tasmania, which lie in the 
‘Roaring Forties’, a high wind zone.

Travelling by air is the quickest way, and sometimes the only way,

Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
The clothes we wear are made from raw materials such as  
cotton, wool, hemp, nylon and PET plastic. There are energy  
and environmental costs to growing or making these raw  
materials, and manufacturing the fabric adds an 
extra cost. Most clothing is made in countries 
where wages are low, which adds a human 
cost. Washing clothes uses energy and water, 
and when we’re finished with them, throwing 
clothes away adds an environmental cost. 
When all the costs are added up, our clothes 
cost the planet a lot more than the price we 
pay for them.
1 
Over 50% of clothing is made from cotton. Growing and processing cotton uses  
large amounts of pesticides and bleach. Organic, unbleached cotton is grown  
without pesticides and is more sustainable than non-organic varieties.
 
The Venn diagram represents different  
types of T shirts sold in a store. 
 
Set O represents T shirts made with organic cotton. 
Set L represents T shirts made by workers who are 
paid at least enough money to live on (at least a 
living wage). 
a Match one or more of the four shaded areas

Maths in sustainability

The planet we live on has taken 
a very long time to become a 
place where humans can live. 
We take for granted the fact 
that life forms such as air-
breathing, complex organisms 
like humans can exist on Earth. 
It has not always been so. 
For most of the life of our 
planet, conditions have not 
been suitable for any life forms, 
except in the oceans. 
By looking at the immense time scales involved in the evolution of life on Earth, we can see 
how important it is to live sustainably on the planet to keep conditions right for human 
existence. It’s a long way to the next human-habitable planet.
1 
This work sheet is about working with large numbers written in scientific notation.  
A number written in scientific notation has two parts: a number that is one or more,  
but less than ten, multiplied by a power of ten. 
 
For example, we can write ninety six million as a  
basic numeral 96 000 000, or in scientific notation as 9.6 × 107.  
Four thousand can be written as 4000 (basic numeral) or  
4 × 103 (scientific notation).
a Write forty two million as 
i a basic numeral   
ii     a number in scientific notation.
b One billion is one thousand million. Write one billion as 
i a basic numeral   
ii     a number in scientific notation.
c Which of these numbers are correctly written in scientific notation? 
i 2.5 × 104 
 
 
ii     13.6 × 106 
iii 8 × 105  
 
 
iv     0.753 × 108 
2 
Scientists estimate Earth to be four billion, six hundred million years old.
a Write this number as a basic numeral.
b Fill in the gaps to write the age of Earth as a number in scientific notation:   
 4.     × 10

d Scientists believe that a collision between Earth and  
a second planet named Theia led to the moon being formed.  
This happened four point five billion, or 4.     × 10    years ago.
e How long after Earth formed did the collision happen? Write the answer   
i in words  
ii     as a basic numeral  
iii     as a number in scientific notation.

which lasted from 2420 million years ago to 541 million years ago.

i as a basic numeral  
ii     in scientific notation.

years ago). Almost all life on Earth became extinct due to a large rise in CO2 in the 
atmosphere. Massive eruptions of lava in Siberia are thought to have been responsible.
a The eruptions produced 1.5 million cubic kilometres of lava.  
Write this in scientific notation.

How many cubic metres are there in one cubic kilometre?

(3600 seconds = 1 hour, 24 hours = 1 day, 365 days = 1 year).

(5) CLIMATE AND WEATH

To complete this topic, students will need:
* to write answers on 8 separate sheet or in a workbook
* Internet access

*7 climate graph templates per small group for Question 4 - see inside back cover.

‘Weather is what you get and climate is what you
expect,’ This is a common description of how to
remember the difference. Two of the most common
conditions that are graphed are mean temperature
and precipitation, which are displayed either in a
tabular form or as a climatic graph (also referred
to as a climograph). The combined line and bar
graph allows for a quick, generalised assessment
of the average climate for a specific place.

DEFINITIONS
weather is the combination of atmospheric
elements such as temperature, precipitation and
humidity that occur at a specific time and place
climate describes the same atmospheric
conditions that have been averaged over a long
period - often 30 years or more

mean = the average of a set of measurements

The number of ecosystems on Earth and the
biodiversity within them are indicators of the
health of the natural environment. Ecosystems
range in size from very small, such as a rock
pool or a rotting log, to those that cover large
areas, such as a coral reef or a forest. The living
and non-living parts in an ecosystem interact to
make it function and stay strong. If one or more
of the parts is damaged, then the ecosystem
itself is also threatened with damage.

DEFINITIONS

an ecosystem is a community of living organisms
and their physical environment, such as soil, air,
water, vegetation

biodiversity is the variety of living things — plants,
animals, insects, water creatures and bacteria
coral bleaching occurs where living coral has
been killed through high water temperatures

to synthesise is to put together various elements
into a whole explanation

health of the natural environment. Ecosystems

species are currently listed as nationally threatened: Blue Whale (endangered), Southern Right Whale
(endangered), Sei Whale (vulnerable), Fin Whale (vulnerable), and Humpback Whale (vulnerable).
Under the Commonwealth Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 all cetaceans
(whales, dolphins and porpoises) are protected in Australian waters, Within this zone it is an offence to
kill, injure or interfere with a cetacean.

In 2001 more than 50 per cent of the world’s
population lived within 150 kilometres of the
coast. This was projected to increase to

75 per cent by 2025. Also in 2001, one in five -
3.6 million — Australians was a provincial coastal
city or town dweller. The population of non-
metropolitan coastal Australia is predicted to
rise to 4.3 million by 2020.

8 provincial city or town is a large urban place
outside a capital city

non-metropolitan is outside a capital city
metropolitan area

great influence

1 Read the text below, then draw a multiple bar graph that reflects the data provided in it. Add a title,

The third Australian culture - from the bush to the burbs to the beach

by Bernard Salt

The first 200 years of white settlement yielded two distinctive
Australian cultures: the bush and the city. A third culture
‘emerged in the latter decades of the 20th century and remains
ascendant ~ the culture of the beach. At the turn of the 20th
century there were 3.8 million people of various backgrounds
on the Australian continent, About 2.3 million of these lived in
inland and rural areas.

The capital cities then contained barely 1.2 million
collectively. The balance lived on the coast in port-based cities.
By the turn of the 2ist century, the number in the bush had
increased to 3.3 million, while the number in the capital cities
had skyrocketed to 12.5 million. The balance of 3.6 million
lived in coastal towns and cities. This collection of around 3
million people linked by a common geography is more than
sufficient to exert an influence over the culture of a nation
with fewer than 20 million.

At the time of Federation, the bush ruled: the swagman, the
squatter, corked hats and windmills defined the Australian
nation. But during the 20th century, things changed. The total
number living in the bush did not dectine; rather the number
living elsewhere increased at a faster rate.

This led to the rise of a distinctive second Australian culture
— the culture of the city, or more precisely, the culture of
suburbia.

But in the latter part of the 20th century, Australians forged
a new ternitory within their island continent ~ the beach
Facilitated by new values and concepts such as leisure,
entertainment, lifestyle and retirement and aided by new
social and financial arrangements such as superannuation,
Australians began clustering in large numbers along the coast
and in most parts of the well-watered edges of the continent:
along the eastern seaboard, across the Fleurieu Peninsula of
South Australia, and along the length of the south-west cape
of Western Australia,

This third Australian culture is now a critical mass. This
non-metropolitan piece of Australian geography contained 3.6
million people out of a total of 19.4 million at June 2001, up
from less than 300 000 one century before. This third
Australian culture will remain a powerful force for decades to
come, especially during the early years of the 21st century as
baby boomers greet retirement from 2006 and seek their own
version of ‘suburbia by the sea’,

GIVING AID TO OTHERS

In your own community there are ways that
people are helped if they have a lower standard
of living than most, At the state and national
level in Australia, financial and other types of
assistance are sometimes provided to areas in
special need. At the international level, many of
the richer nations provide foreign aid on a
yearly basis to countries in need. A major aim of
foreign aid is to try to increase the quality of life
of some regions, and narrow the gap between
the rich and the poor. NGOs also provide aid at
the international level.

1 All people have basic needs that must be met so
that they can survive. They also have basic wants
that help make life healthier, safer and more

The victims of the tsunami pay the
price of war on Iraq

The US government has so far pledged $350m to the
victims of the tsunami, and the UK government $96m, The
US has spent $148 billion on the Iraq war and the UK
$11.5bn. The war has been running for 656 days. This
‘means that the money pledged for the tsunami disaster by
the United States is the equivalent of one and a half day's
spending in Iraq. The money the UK has given equates to
five and a half days of involvement in the war.

It looks still worse when you compare the cost of the
‘war to the total foreign aid budget. The UK has spent
almost twice as much on creating suffering in Iraq as it
spends annually on relieving it elsewhere. The United
States gives just over $16bn in foreign aid: less than one
ninth of the money it has burnt so far in Iraq.

‘The figures for war and aid are worth comparing
because, when all the other excuses for the invasion of Iraq
were stripped away, both governments explained that it was
being waged for the good of the Iraqis.

To justify the war, even under these wildly unsafe
assumptions, George Bush and Tony Blair would have to
show that the money they spent was a means of relieving
human suffering. As there are more than 2.8 billion people
living in absolute poverty, and as there are only 25 million
people in frag, this is simply not possible.

Even within the official aid budgets the two aims are
confused: $8.9bn of the aid money the US spends is used
for military assistance, anti-drugs operations, counter-
terrorism and the Iraq relief and reconstruction fund,

Source: Adapted from an article by George Monbiot in
The Guardian, 4 January 2005

(iJ AGRAMS IN GEOGRAP

When you study Geography, you learn about
earth’s natural features - land, water, and plant
and animal life. You also look at places and
things people have built and try to understand
how and why they are different, and what effect
they have had on natural things. You’ve probably
heard the saying: ‘A picture’s worth a thousand
words’. Pictures in Geography are called
diagrams. Diagrams in Geography are graphic
organisers that help you understand more about
Planet Earth and how people live on it and
interact with it.

DEFINITIONS
Geography is the study of Earth as the place
where people live

diagrams are special types of drawings that show
models of things in real life, or how things work,
or steps in a process, or how things are organised

to interact is when two or more things act on

each other by coming into contact

the built environment is what people have made
or grown

the natural environment is all the living and non-
living parts of Earth that have been formed by
nature

part of a large planet in one of the solar systems
of the universe. Earth is the third planet from
the Sun at a distance of about 150 million
kilometres. Earth is the fifth largest planet out of
the nine known planets in our solar system.
Earth’s diameter is about 12 750 kilometres,
compared to the Sun’s diameter of 1 392 000
kilometres. Earth has one moon, which is about
one-quarter the size of Earth.

Earth’s layers

Millions of years ago Earth was molten rock. Then the outer surface cooled and became solid. However,
under the top layers, it still remains very, very hot. Scientists have been able to learn about the
different layers that make up Earth’s mass by studying earthquakes and volcanoes.

Layer

Descripton

Crust

The hard and rocky outer surface of
Earth, which is thinner under the
oceans. The crust’s thickness ranges
between 6 and 75 kilometres. It is
made up mostly of water, and different
types of rocks and minerals.
Temperatures on the crust’s surface
range from below zero to about 50°C,
and up to 870°C near the boundary
with the mantle.

Mantle

The rocky layer that extends just over
2800 kilometres. It is made up of
silicon, oxygen, magnesium, iron,
aluminium and calcium. The part of the
mantle closest to the surface is rigid,
but lower down it flows slowly - a few
centimetres each year. Temperatures
range for 1000°C at the boundary with
the crust to 2200°C at the boundary
with the core.

Outer core

The molten layer made up mostly of
iron and nickel that surrounds the
inner core. Its thickness averages
around 2280 kilometres. Temperatures
range between 2200 and 4500°C.

Inner core

The centre of Earth made up of solid
iron and nickel. It is extremely hot with
temperatures over 4500°C up to
7200°C. It is also under great pressure.
Its radius is about 1230 kilometres.

Earth’s atmosphere

The ozone layer

containing three atoms of oxygen - its chemical formula is 03. (The formula of oxygen gas is O>.) The
ozone layer blocks most of the harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun. There is evidence that
the ozone layer is getting thinner due to chemical emissions from human activity on Earth.

Pictures from satellites circling above show
Planet Earth as a beautiful blue ball that is
surrounded by trails of clouds. We can also see
clouds when we look up from ground level. They
are formed when water vapour condenses on
extremely tiny particles floating in the
troposphere. Clouds move with wind currents.
Different types of clouds form because of
different conditions in the atmosphere from
place to place. Fog is a form of cloud that makes
contact with the ground.

(7J RIVER SYSTEM

If you were flying high in outer space looking
down on Earth, you could see a pattern of veins
branching out over the land surface. This pattern
is formed by the thousands of different streams
and rivers that make their way from highlands to
larger bodies of water - inland lakes, and the
seas and oceans. As soon as rain falls on the
ground or snow melts, water starts moving
downhill. At the source the flow is only a trickle,
then it becomes bigger and stronger as it travels
down steep slopes to flatter land. The river is
joined by tributaries, which add to its volume.

dimensions - length, width and depth

meanders are winding parts of rivers on flat land

an estuary is the part of a river close to the sea
where fresh and saltwater mix

the mouth of a river is where it spills into the sea

a delta is a nearly flat plain deposited between
branches of the mouth of a river

Most school atlases have a world map showing
the main tectonic plates that make up Earth’s
crust. Scientists think the plates were caused by
cracking when Planet Earth cooled millions and
millions of years ago. The continents and oceans
are floating on these huge plates. They rest on
Earth’s hot mantle. So far 7 large and about 20
smaller plates have been marked out and
named. The plates are separated by fault lines.
The movement between plates and along faults
is jerky and can cause earthquakes. There are
three main types of tectonic movement.

THE MovING EARTH

DEFINITIONS
a continent is one of the seven huge land masses
that Earth can be divided into

tectonic means something do with Earth’s crust

a tectonic plate is a huge sheet of rock between 6
and 75 kilometres thick that lies under part of a

continent or one of the oceans

a fault is a break in a mass of rock causing
disturbance along the crack

subduction occurs when an oceanic plate slides
under a lighter continental plate

Divergent boundary

Convergent boundary

Transform boundary

You can simulate divergent plate
motion by placing your palms
down with your index fingers
touching. Now pull your

hands apart.

You can simulate convergent
plate motion by placing your
hands together in front of you
with your palms down. Gently
slide your left hand downward
and your right hand upward but
keep them in contact.

You can simulate transformational
plate motion by placing your hands
together in front of you with your
palms down. Now slide your right
hand away from you and your left
hand toward you in the same plane.

ESERT LANDFORMS

Across the globe there are many dry areas that
receive 250 millimetres or less total annual
precipitation. Deserts can be hot or cold. In hot
deserts the wind and rain form the land into
different shapes. Although there is not much
water, when it falls it is usually in heavy storms.
Rain strikes the hard ground. It does not have
time to soak in so runs off in wild torrents
causing a lot of erosion. The wind in deserts is
usually strong and contains millions of sand or

DEFINITIONS

a torrent is a large volume of fast-moving water

precipitation is all types of water that reach
Earth’s surface either as a liquid (rain, dew) or
solid (snow, hail, frost)

erosion occurs when the land is worn away by
running water and blowing wind

deposition occurs when eroded material is carried
away and then settles in a new place

rock particles, which also cause erosion. Eroded
material is then deposited. Desert landforms are
the result of this erosion and deposition.

Profiles are diagrams that show the hidden parts
of a geographic feature by viewing a model from
side on. They are similar to cross-sections.
Profiles are often used to show different layers
of vegetation in a forest or the horizons of a
particular soil. Changes to the profile over a
period of time can indicate changes in the
environment, especially the impact of humans
on the environment.

animals extending over large natural areas

Soil is the very top thin layer of Earth’s crust, ranging from a few centimetres to several metres thick.

Gallipoli and the Anzacs 
1
Since 1915, one day in the year has involved the whole of Australia in solemn ceremonies of 
remembrance, gratitude and national pride. That day is Anzac Day – 25 April.
Ten weeks after the beginning of World War 1, Australia and New Zealand sent 30 000 troops 
to Egypt for combat training. It was here that the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps 
acronym ANZAC was first used. At 3 am, on April 25 1914 just off the shores of Gallipoli in 
Turkey, in an area later to be known as Anzac Cove, three battleships gathered full of Anzac 
soldiers about to head into history. HMAS Queen, HMAS London and HMAS Prince of Wales 
released 48 boats or ‘tows’ at 3.30 am and the landings continued from 5.30 to 7.30 am. But 
something went wrong. The landings were over 2 km north of the intended area – a 6 km 
stretch of beach from about 1.6 km north of Gaba Tepe to a point near Fisherman’s Hut.

Hard tack and the Anzacs 
2
Besides the constant fear of death on the hills and dunes of Gallipoli, some logistical challenges 
included feeding the soldiers. Food supplies came from as far away as Greece and Egypt and 
perishables just wouldn’t survive. The soldiers’ food came in tins with the staples being corned beef 
(Bully Beef), rice, tea, cocoa, jam and ‘hard tack’. Hard tack is basically a very hard biscuit made 
of flour, water, salt and sugar. It lasts longer than bread, although it was so hard soldiers would 
sometimes break their teeth trying to eat it.
Unlike bread, hard tack biscuits are very, very hard. Some soldiers preferred to grind them up 
with old ammunition shells, mix them with water and eat it as porridge. 
The recipe below has been based on a recipe used during World War 1.
Ingredients (makes six biscuits)
• 190 g white flour 
• 375 g wholemeal flour 
• 40 g sugar 
• 21 g milk powder 
• good pinch salt 
• 220 ml water

water is 220 ml.

a  3 tablespoons? 
b 6 tablespoons?

became the Royal Australian Army Nursing Corps (RAANC). The RAANC were formed to care for

wherever Australian and British troops served. Approximately 2140 served overseas, 420 
served in Australia, 25 died and 390 were decorated.

Red Cross

Australian Red Cross was formed on 13 August 1914 exactly nine days after the outbreak of World 
War I. Lady Munro-Ferguson, who had worked for British Red Cross in Scotland and was the wife of 
the Governor-General, called on the wives of each State Governor to form a local committee in each 
capital. The women readily agreed and so Australian Red Cross was born.
During World War 2, Red Cross transported 40 000 pairs of socks, 25 000 shirts, 20 000 
underpants, 10 000 pairs of shoes and boots, 10 000 pairs of pyjamas, 5000 overcoats and 
many other items people thought would be useful to soldiers on the front in Europe. The effort 
from many small communities ‘beggared the imagination’. By the end of the war Red Cross 
unit of Rutherglen had forwarded, among many other items, more than 1200 shirts, 8500 
pairs of underpants, 1200 pairs of pyjamas, 2400 pairs of socks, 75 sheets, 770 pillow-cases, 
450 bed sheets and 390 handkerchiefs.

The Battle of the Coral Sea was actually a series of battles that pitted the forces of the United 
States and Australia against the Japanese on 4–8 May, 1942. This significant naval battle halted 
the seaborne invasion of Port Moresby by the Japanese. The ships did not engage in direct battle. It 
was a naval battle fought entirely by aircraft using the vessels as runways.

The Kokoda Trail 
7
In World War 2, the Japanese army had advanced through Asia en route to Australia. Port Moresby, 
the capital of Papua New Guinea, was a significant base for both armies. Had the Japanese set up 
base in Port Moresby the Australian mainland would have been under severe threat of invasion. 
The Kokoda track was a seldom-used trail from the small coastal village of Buna on the north coast 
of Papua over the Owen Stanley Ranges to Port Moresby, passing through the village of Kokoda. In 
1942 the Japanese tried to capture Port Moresby by sea attack and then overland through Kokoda. 
The seven-month resistance of this ultimately unsuccessful campaign is regarded by some as one of 
the most heroic defensive actions in military history by an Australian force.

The Rats of Tobruk 
8
During World War 2, North Africa became a place of strategic importance to the Allied and German 
forces due to its position as a supply route. The Allied forces in North Africa included troops from 
Britain, Australia, New Zealand, United States and India. German troops were joined in their fight 
against the Allied forces by the Italian army.
• September 1940: Germans invade 
Egypt 
• January 1941: Australians capture 
Tobruk and its port 
• March 1941: Germans defeat 
Australians at El Agheila in Libya
• April 1941: Germans capture Libya 
(except for Tobruk)

Allies had more than 200 000 men and more than 1000 tanks. This battle cost the Allied 
forces nearly 13 500 men; Germans and Italians lost 25 000 soldiers. The battle lasted for 13 
days.

of Rommel – the leader of the German and Italian Army in North Africa. 124 tanks attacked

The Allied forces began damaging the supply lines to Rommel so that only 33% of what 
Rommel needed was getting through to him. During June he received 5000 tonnes of supplies

described the Australians as ‘caught like rats in a trap’. The Australians managed to hold off 
the German forces for 250 days.

days in a month)?

Little Boy and Fat Man 
9
During the final stages of World War 2, the United States dropped two atomic bombs over the 
Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in a successful attempt to hasten the end of the war. The 
nuclear weapon known as ‘Little Boy’ was dropped over Hiroshima on August 6 1945. ‘Fat Man’ was 
released over Nagasaki on August 9 of the same year.
The capture of Tinian, one of the Marianas Islands, provided American forces with a valuable 
airstrip from which to mount raids on Japan. The islands served as the base from which the 
atomic bomb attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were staged.
1 
Colour the seas, nations and islands different colours.
2

a Tinian 
b Nagasaki 
c Sapporo.
3

b 16°N, 146°E 
c 45°N, 129°E
Hiroshima was the primary target of the first nuclear 
bombing mission on August 6. A B-29 bomber was 
launched from Tinian in the west Pacific, about six 
hours flight time from Japan. Two other B-29s were also 
launched. After leaving Tinian the aircraft made their 
way separately to Iwo Jima where they met at an altitude 
of 2440 metres and set course for Japan. The aircraft 
arrived over the target in clear visibility at 9855 metres. 
4

Japan.
5

return trip.
6

7

a   Iwo Jima? 
b  Hiroshima?
8

9 
Why do think the bombers increased their altitude at Hiroshima?
The gravity bomb known as ‘Little Boy’ was released at 8.15 am from a height of  
 
9855 metres.  ‘Little Boy’ contained 60 kilograms of uranium-235 and took 57 seconds to 
fall from the aircraft to the predetermined detonation height about 600 m above the city. 
It created a blast equivalent to about 13 kilotons of TNT. The uranium-235 weapon was 
considered very inefficient, with only 1.38% of its material exploding.

At the time of the attack the population of Hiroshima was approximately 345 000. 
Approximately 80 000 people were killed immediately and another 70 000 were injured. It has 
been estimated that, of the people who died on the day of the explosion, 60% died from burns, 
30% from falling bricks, timber and other materials and 10% from other causes. 
18 Find the total number of people who were killed or injured by the blast.

immediately by the blast?

a  flash or flame burns?

On the morning of August 9 1945, the nuclear bomb code-named Fat Man was detonated. 
The bomb contained 6.4 kg of plutonium-239, and was dropped on Nagasaki’s industrial 
valley at 11.01 am. The estimated population of Nagasaki at the time of the bombing was 270 
000. Fat Man exploded 43 seconds later at 469 m above the ground. 
21 What was the time when Fat Man exploded?
22 Using the 24-hour clock, what time was Fat Man dropped?
23 Of the total population of Nagasaki, calculate the percentage of immediate deaths if   
60 000 people were killed in the blast.
24 How many grams of plutonium-239 were contained in ‘Fat Man’?
On August 15, six days after the detonation over Nagasaki, Japan announced its surrender to 
the Allied Powers. They signed the Instrument of Surrender on September 2, officially ending 
the Pacific War and therefore World War 2.
25 After the bombing of Nagasaki, how many hours did it take for the Japanese to 
surrender?

Time lines are examples of number lines. The dates of events are arranged in ascending order, 
left to right. A suitable scale should be used to indicate the correct gaps between the dates.
This time line shows the dates of key events in the history of China.
1 
In which year was
a Kublai Khan declared Emperor of China?
b the Qing dynasty established?
c Hong Kong ceded to Britain?
d the People’s Republic of China proclaimed?
2 
Which event happened earlier – A or B?
 
A Hong Kong was ceded to Britain.
 
B  Portugal was granted Macao  
(a small peninsula in southern China).
3 
a In which year was the Ming dynasty established?
b In which year did the Ming dynasty end?
c How many years did the Ming dynasty last? 
4 
How many years did the Qing dynasty last?
5 
How many years after Kublai Khan  
was declared Emperor 
a was the Ming dynasty established?
b was the Qing dynasty established?
c did China become a republic?
6 
Hong Kong was handed back to China in 1997.  
How many years did British rule last in Hong Kong?

Papua New Guinea is home to a large number  
of species of birds. 
The bird-of-paradise is universally identified with the  
island of New Guinea. An adult bird-of-paradise is  
depicted on the national flag of Papua New Guinea.
There are 44 species of birds-of-paradise worldwide  
and 35 species are found in Papua New Guinea.  
A few species are also found in surrounding islands  
and north-eastern Australia.
The smallest bird-of-paradise in size is the  
King Bird-of-paradise which on average has  
a mass of 50 g and is 15 cm long. 
The Curl-crested Manucode is 44 cm long  
and has a mass of 430 g.
The male Black Sicklebill, with its long tail,  
is the longest bird-of-paradise species at 110 cm.
1 
What fraction of the 44 species of  
birds-of-paradise are found in  
Papua New Guinea?
2 
Express the average mass of a King  
Bird-of-paradise as a fraction of the  
average mass of a Curl-crested Manucode.  
Simplify your answer.
3 
Express the length of a Curl-crested  
Manucode as a fraction of the length of  
a male Black Sicklebill. Simplify your answer. 
4 
Express the length of a King Bird-of-paradise as a percentage of the length  
of a male Black Sicklebill. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place. 
There are many other types of birds found in New Guinea.
The Papuan Eagle (also known as the Kapul Eagle) has an average length of 83 cm.  
Its wingspan measures 157 cm and its average mass is 2 000 g.
The Palm Cockatoo has an average mass of 1 060 g.
5 
a  Express the average mass of a Palm Cockatoo as a fraction of the average mass  
of a Papuan Eagle. Simplify your answer. 
b Write this answer as a percentage. 
6 
The Palm Cockatoo is about 7 
10 of the length of a Papuan Eagle. 
 
What is the average length of a Palm Cockatoo?  
Answer to the nearest centimetre.

The Blue-faced Honeyeater has distinctive plumage,  
with olive upperparts, white underparts and a black  
head and throat with white nape and cheeks. It is an  
average 30 cm in length and has a wingspan of 44 cm.
The average length of a Papuan King Parrot is 36 cm,  
including a long broad tail.
7

a fraction of the length of a Papuan King Parrot.  
Simplify your answer. 
8

as a percentage of the wingspan of a Papuan  
Eagle (157 cm). Give your answer correct to  
1 decimal place.

What is the mass of a Blue-faced Honeyeater?  
The Forest Kingfisher has blue wings, head and tail with white breast, abdomen and nape.  
It has an average length of 23.5 cm.
The male Golden Monarch Flycatcher is a bright golden colour with sharply delineated black 
cheeks and throat, primary wing feathers and tail. It has an average length of 13.5 cm.
10 Express the average length of a Golden Monarch Flycatcher as a fraction of the average 
length of a Forest Kingfisher. Simplify your answer. 
11 Express the average length of a Forest Kingfisher as a percentage of the average length  
of a Golden Monarch Flycatcher. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place. 
12 Express the length of a King Bird-of-paradise (15 cm) as a percentage of the length  
of a Forest Kingfisher. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
There are 35 species of bird-of-paradise found in New Guinea. They include the Superb  
Bird-of-paradise, the Emperor Bird-of-paradise and the Yellow Breasted Bird-of-paradise. 
The average length of an Emperor Bird-of-paradise is 33 cm. 
13 A Yellow Breasted Bird-of-paradise is approximately 2 
3 the length  
of an Emperor Bird-of-paradise.  
How long is a Yellow Breasted Bird-of-paradise?
14 A Superb Bird-of-paradise is approximately 80% of the length of an  
Emperor Bird-of-paradise. How long is a Superb Bird-of-paradise?  
Give your answer to the nearest centimetre.
15 A Raggiana Bird-of-paradise is more than twice the length of a King Bird-of-paradise  
(15 cm long). The King Bird-of-paradise is approximately 44% of the length of the 
Raggiana Bird-of-paradise. 
 
How long is a Raggiana Bird-of-paradise? Give your answer to the nearest centimetre.
